title: The US, Iran, Israel, and the future of the Middle East
subtitle: US strategic ambiguity in Iran has failed
author: Christian Emery
introduction: The Middle East is ablaze. But with the recent escalation between Iran and Israel, where do the sources of escalation lie? And what historical mistakes do we need to understand to forge a path to peace? University College London's, Christian Emery, argues that this escalation is a failure of America's restraint. The US's rightful fear of a regional war has restrained its might. But now is the time for Trump to make a firm commitment in either direction. Strategic ambiguity has failed, and the world now waits for Trump to decide its fate.
body:
What began as a devastating but targeted Israeli strike on Iran’s nuclear programme and senior military leadership on 13 June has, with bleak predictability, escalated into both sides striking densely populated areas indiscriminately. Israel is now issuing an impossible warning to Tehran’s residents—one chillingly familiar to the civilians of Gaza and Lebanon: leave, or face death or injury. Both sides are vowing to inflict a heavy human cost, but the imbalance in military power means only Israel—thanks to its total air superiority—can carry out large-scale airstrikes largely at will. Iran must ration its remaining supply of ballistic missiles, but it still has escalatory options that could significantly raise the cost of this war to the global community, though this comes with serious risks.

Israel is unlikely to achieve its two stated war aims—eliminating Iran’s entire nuclear and ballistic missile production capacity, let alone its fantastical aim of regime change—without U.S. assistance.

How we arrived at this disastrous war is as much a story of the failure of U.S. restraint as it is of Israel’s reckless calculation that this is the moment to eliminate, once and for all, the threat of a nuclear Iran—and perhaps even the regime itself. Indeed, now Israel has crossed the Rubicon, where America’s commitment to restraint now stands requires the more urgent analysis. This is because, by day five of the war, it’s clear that despite the stark asymmetry in military capabilities between Iran and Israel, Israel is unlikely to achieve its two stated war aims—eliminating Iran’s entire nuclear and ballistic missile production capacity, let alone its fantastical aim of regime change—without U.S. assistance. Drawing the U.S. into the conflict, is thus a central part of Israel’s strategy.

There are two possible routes for Israel to draw the U.S. into this war. The first is to tempt Trump into believing that, now Israel has systematically dismantled Iran’s air defences, U.S. bombers could strike unopposed, and after a few sorties dropping 30,000-pound bunker-buster bombs, Trump can claim credit for permanently destroying Iran’s nuclear capabilities. Iran withdrawing from the Non-Proliferation Treaty and formally ending all cooperation with the IAEA could provide some political cover for doing so.

The second, and more likely, route involves Israel continuing to pummel Iran with impunity—potentially targeting critical water and electricity infrastructure—until Iran feels it has no option but to escalate despite the risks. This might involve attacking Gulf shipping or refineries, or even attempting to block the Strait of Hormuz, in turn compelling the U.S. to intervene in its longstanding role as guarantor of maritime security in the Persian Gulf.

Iran has quickly recognised the extreme risk of drawing the U.S. into the conflict. This is why it has so far refrained from authorising its proxies to target U.S. personnel or threaten Gulf shipping, and why it is reportedly sending messages to Washington saying it wants a ceasefire and offering to resume nuclear talks—on the condition that America stays out of the war.

Twenty years of restraint

Since the discovery of undeclared Iranian nuclear sites in 2003, Israel has asked every American president since George W. Bush to green light an Israeli attack on Iran with American support. All have refused for more or less the same reasons: they didn’t believe a strike could permanently disable Iran’s nuclear facilities, and feared it would spiral into a wider conflict, pulling in the US and its allies while wreaking havoc on the global economy.

Trump’s inability to follow a coherent long-term strategy—or to fully grasp the consequences of his actions—was then, as it is now, a major liability for America’s credibility.

True, the U.S. is less vulnerable to Iranian retaliation than it once was. In part, this reflects the significant draw-down of America’s footprint in the region and the significant degradation of Iranian regional proxies who might attack US personnel or facilities. Back in 2008, when George Bush warned against an Israeli strike—despite reportedly coming close to launching one himself two years earlier—there were more than 150,000 American troops in Iraq, and Iran’s Shia proxies were in the midst of a brutal insurgency against them. When Obama signed the Iranian nuclear deal known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) in 2015, the US was still several years away from winkling ISIS out of Syria and Iraq; and one of his strongest arguments was that resolving the Iranian nuclear issue was vital to that effort. Indeed, the central strategic rationale behind the JCPOA was that, amid a major global economic crisis, the costly failure in Iraq, and a growing desire to pivot toward containing China, a regional war involving Iran would be disastrous.

Trump’s decision to wreck the JCPOA in 2018 has proved to be one of the biggest mistakes in recent US foreign policy and is a key reason for the failure of American restraint now. Trump was advised that crushing the Iranian economy would either force the regime to accept major restrictions on its nuclear programme and moderate its regional behaviour or cause the entire system to collapse. This was despite all the other JCPOA signatories, and indeed most Americans, believing that the deal was the best way to prevent Iran from crossing the threshold required for nuclear weapons.

Instead, what followed almost immediately was a sharp escalation of tensions in the Persian Gulf, attacks on U.S. personnel by Iran-backed Shia proxies, greater Iranian reliance on those proxies, and a massive increase in its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

However, anyone inclined to credit Biden should recognise that he failed to apply any meaningful restraint to Netanyahu’s campaign of ethnic cleansing in Gaza—in fact, the Israeli leader likely leveraged muted U.S. disapproval over Gaza in exchange for some degree of restraint against Iran.

Having needlessly provoked a major regional crisis, Iran responded to his maximum pressure campaign and the assassination of General Qasem Soleimani by harassing shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, attacking U.S. forces in Iraq, and striking Saudi oil infrastructure, Trump made it abundantly clear he had no appetite for a major confrontation—especially in an election year. Trump’s inability to follow a coherent long-term strategy—or to fully grasp the consequences of his actions—was then, as it is now, a major liability for America’s credibility.

Trump supporters will point out that the first direct shooting war between Iran and Israel broke out under President Biden. But despite lacking the warm relationship with Netanyahu that Trump enjoys, Biden managed to rein in Israeli action from a full-scale assault—likely resembling what we’re seeing now—to more limited strikes, mostly focused on air defence and missile production facilities outside populated areas. However, anyone inclined to credit Biden should recognise that he failed to apply any meaningful restraint to Netanyahu’s campaign of ethnic cleansing in Gaza—in fact, the Israeli leader likely leveraged muted U.S. disapproval over Gaza in exchange for some degree of restraint against Iran.

Trump’s bumbling crisis management

When Israel and Iran last exchanged fire in October 2024, Biden made it clear that while he supported Israel’s right to retaliate and committed U.S. military assets to help intercept Iranian counterstrikes, the U.S. would not participate in offensive action. At the same time, Washington briefed the press that the U.S. had vetoed anything beyond a limited Israeli strike.

Five days in, we still have no clear sense of where the Trump administration stands on this war. Shortly after the Israeli attack began last Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a firm line: Israel had informed the U.S. in advance, but this was a unilateral Israeli strike. The U.S. was not involved, and therefore Iran should not retaliate against American forces. Yet just hours later, Trump—desperate to avoid the appearance that Israel had torpedoed his diplomatic push for a new nuclear deal—gave the exact opposite impression. He essentially told reporters that the strike had been coordinated with the U.S., and that he had used Israel’s advance warning to pressure Iran into making major concessions ahead of the planned talks in Oman.

It will be difficult for historians to find a more risible snapshot of an American president so out of his depth—so morally and intellectually untethered from even the lowest demands of statecraft—than Trump posting on his own social media that his best solution to the current crisis is for 10 million Iranians to somehow evacuate Tehran.

Iran had indeed been concerned about the possibility of an Israeli attack, but the announcement of the first high-level U.S.–Iran talks in nearly eight years had reassured them it was unlikely to happen while diplomacy was underway. As a result, they did not place their military on high alert or move key political and military leaders to secure locations.

Trump, unable to resist recentering himself into the whole situation, only managed to give the impression that he had been part of an elaborate disinformation campaign designed to lull Iran into dropping its guard ahead of a surprise Israeli attack. When it is equally plausible, he was simply duped by the Israelis into convincing Iran the strike wouldn’t happen. At some point, it likely became clear to him that this was, at best, a disastrous strategy for anyone hoping to broker a future deal with Tehran, and at worst, a green light for Iran to view U.S. targets as legitimate. So, by Sunday, Trump was insisting that the U.S. "had nothing to do" with Israel’s strikes on Iran, despite U.S. officials already confirming they were assisting Israel in intercepting incoming ballistic missiles. On the same day he declared “we will have peace, soon, between Israel and Iran” offering no explanation of how he intended to achieve this, only complaining that he hadn’t received enough credit for his diplomatic efforts. The next day he denied he was working towards a ceasefire.

It will be difficult for historians to find a more risible snapshot of an American president so out of his depth—so morally and intellectually untethered from even the lowest demands of statecraft—than Trump posting on his own social media that his best solution to the current crisis is for 10 million Iranians to somehow evacuate Tehran.

Trump’s baffling approach to crisis management offers little clarity on whether America might seek to try to put pressure on both sides to at least pause hostilities. If Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu has a clear plan for drawing in the US, Trump’s performance so far doesn’t inspire confidence that he can frustrate it. Then again, Netanyahu’s unrelentingly ruthless determination to pursue what he believes best serves either Israel’s security or his own political survival inspires little confidence that he would defer to Washington on any significant aspect of this campaign.

But any clear-eyed analysis of not just US interests, but the separate but related examination of Trump’s personal interests, leads to the inescapable conclusion that this war is a disastrous outcome. It’s precisely why so many American presidents, including Trump himself only recently, have tried to forestall it.

The obvious case for a ceasefire

When Trump came back into power, he was strangely reticent about Iran, despite his historical antagonism towards the country and the extraordinary accusation that Iranian agents had planned to assassinate him. Many expected Trump to double down on the maximum pressure policy of crippling sanctions and threats that had characterised his first administration. Yet his priorities seemed instead to be trashing America’s relationship with its closest allies, and he unexpectedly fired his former special envoy for Iran, Brian Hook, who was widely seen as the architect of the ‘maximum pressure’ policy. Trump seemed to want to cast himself as the peacemaker, and following a personal letter to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in April, he dispatched his most trusted negotiator, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, to try to hammer out a new nuclear deal.

In other words, Trump clearly understood that resolving the nuclear issue was key to preventing a regional war. This was exactly what he was also hearing from his Gulf allies—particularly the Saudis, with whom he maintained close personal ties after leaving office in 2020. The Saudis themselves had concluded that making peace with Iran was essential to the success of their ambitious Vision 2030 economic diversification programme. Ironically, it was Trump’s shocking abandonment of them—after Iranian attacks on Saudi oil processing facilities temporarily shut down 50% of their oil production—that helped convince Riyadh of the strategic necessity of restoring relations with Iran in 2023.

The defining MAGA approach to foreign policy is that the U.S. has spent far too much time and money on other people’s wars.

Trump is also personally financially invested in the Gulf, and seems to view the Saudis and other Gulf states not just as allies, but as equal partners in reshaping the region, treating them as global actors in their own right. He demonstrated his willingness to follow the Saudi lead by backing a deal with a Syrian regime led by a radical—albeit reforming—jihadist, and lifting all sanctions with the stroke of a pen, much to Israel’s alarm, it must be said. In short, Trump’s vision for the Middle East is commercially driven, and he is entirely comfortable with this coming without any meaningful progress on political or human rights.

A war between Iran and Israel not only undermines Trump’s regional goals; it also poses serious domestic risks. The defining MAGA approach to foreign policy is that the U.S. has spent far too much time and money on other people’s wars, and that those resources should be redirected to protecting America’s borders and cutting taxes. Already, some leading MAGA figures—including Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene—are warning Trump that his base does not support foreign intervention. Even more perilous are the economic risks: Trump has promised to cut Americans’ energy bills by 50% within a year—an ambitious claim even before the threat of a major disruption to Persian Gulf supply.

Given how dangerous this war is for Trump, why isn’t he using the enormous leverage he claims he has to secure a ceasefire? How has America’s restraining influence over Israel evaporated so completely? At this point, there seem to be three possible explanations, and all point to Trump’s poor judgement and lack of qualifications. First, he has been completely outmanoeuvred by Israel and may genuinely fail to grasp the risks this war poses to his own strategic and political interests. Second, he is seriously entertaining the idea of joining Israel in a coordinated strike to destroy Iran’s deeply buried nuclear facilities. Third, he simply doesn’t know what to do and is stuck lurching between contradictory messages, hoping something turns up that he can take credit for.

All three are, to put it mildly, deeply concerning.

This piece was written on the 17th of June, 2025
